lesson.menu_desc: Reading a status report and writing in the register it is written in -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- The Progress Report
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Cassio Haunholter Xavier da Silva | Lesson 6 -- The Progress Report

listenings.text: I get about eleven of these a month, and I am honest with the teams about how I read them. I read the first paragraph, I read anything marked outstanding, and I read the variance table. That is four minutes. If your bad news is on page three, I will find it in the meeting instead of in the report, and by then I am annoyed and you have lost the chance to frame it. The reports I trust most are the ones where the worst line is near the top, written in plain words, with the action in the same paragraph. Something like: the equipment base has not been signed off, the client review is now scheduled for the ninth, and the drawings have been re-sequenced so that the steel package is not affected. That is three sentences. I know the problem, the date and the mitigation, and I do not need to call anybody.

Every line in that report was true, and that was the problem. Month one said the layout was progressing. Month two said the layout was progressing. In month three somebody asked a direct question and we found out that the layout had been waiting for a soil report since week two. Nothing had been hidden. Nobody had lied. The word progressing had just been doing a lot of work for two months. Since then I ask for one thing in every report, and it takes ten seconds to write. If an item has not moved since the last report, say so, and say what it is waiting for. Not progressing. Waiting for the soil report, requested on the fourteenth, chased twice. A reader can do something with that sentence. A reader can do nothing at all with progressing.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: the difference between the plan and what actually happened
a formal meeting where a design is examined before it goes further

paras: A monthly progress report is written for somebody who was in none of the meetings and has about four minutes. That reader does not want the month. They want the exceptions: what has changed against the baseline, what is outstanding, and what is going to need a decision before the next report. Everything that is going to plan can be said in one line, because going to plan is not news.

This is why reports are written mostly in the passive. The foundation drawings were issued on Friday. Revision C has been approved. The equipment base has not been signed off yet. In a conversation you would name the person, because in a conversation the person is how you know who to ask. On the page, the document is the subject, and the owner lives in the action list at the end, with a date next to the name. The passive is not there to hide anybody. It is there to put the thing that moved at the front of the sentence.

The reports that cause damage are the ones that are technically true and quietly late. A variance of two weeks that is flagged in month one is a scheduling problem. The same two weeks discovered in month three, because each report said work is progressing, is a credibility problem, and credibility is much harder to recover than two weeks. Experienced project managers put the bad line near the top, in plain words, with what is being done about it in the same paragraph.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: A progress report should describe everything that happened during the month, in order.
A report is written for a reader with four minutes: it leads with the exceptions, uses the passive to put the work first, and flags bad news early.
The passive voice is used in reports to avoid saying who is responsible.
